 India's gold hallmarking system is facing fresh questions over the reliability of its regulatory checks. A draft audit by the comptroller and auditor general (CAG) has reportedly found a substantial shortfall in surveillance inspections of registered jewellers and assaying and hallmarking centres (AHCs). Separately, an investigation by Dainik Bhaskar  has reported that gold adulterated with rhenium powder passed routine purity tests and received a 22-carat hallmark.   The two developments point to different weaknesses in the gold certification system. While the CAG has questioned whether the bureau of Indian standards (BIS) conducts enough physical inspections to ensure continued compliance by registered jewellers, the Dainik Bhaskar investigation has raised concerns about whether commonly used testing methods can detect sophisticated forms of adulteration.   According to the reported draft audit findings, BIS failed to conduct the prescribed annual surveillance inspection at more than 83% of registered jewellers during the five-year period from FY20-21 to FY24-25. In FY24-25 alone, BIS inspected only 5,444 of the 28,865 licensed jewellers, leaving 23,421 without a surveillance inspection. This means more than 81% of licence holders were not covered during the year.   The audit also reportedly found a shortfall of about 43.7% in the prescribed surveillance of AHCs, which test jewellery for purity and carry out hallmarking.   The findings are significant because hallmarking is meant to assure consumers that the declared purity of a gold article corresponds to its actual gold content. The system involves the registration of jewellers, testing at recognised AHCs, and the assignment of a unique hallmark unique identification (HUID) number to individual articles.   CAG Questions Post-certification Checks The draft audit reportedly emphasises that surveillance cannot end once a jeweller is registered or an article is hallmarked. Regular inspections and sample testing are necessary to independently establish whether quality standards continue to be met.   BIS is understood to have attributed the inspection shortfall to manpower constraints and difficulties in collecting samples, particularly from geographically remote locations. The regulator also cited disruptions caused by the Covid-19 pandemic during the audit period. However, auditors reportedly found these explanations inadequate.   BIS has maintained that it achieved its surveillance targets in FY25-26, after the period covered by the audit. The regulator has also used contractual personnel for market surveillance, including collecting samples from jewellery outlets, according to reports.   The CAG's concern is not that every jeweller who escaped inspection was necessarily selling impure gold. Rather, the audit points to a regulatory blind spot: when inspections are not conducted, the regulator has limited independent evidence to establish whether hallmarking standards are being consistently maintained.   The draft report was reportedly sent to the Union ministry of consumer affairs, food and public distribution for comments in July 2026. It is expected to be placed before Parliament after the government's response is incorporated and the audit process is completed. The findings described here are from a draft report and should not be treated as final CAG conclusions.   Dainik Bhaskar Investigation Raises Concerns over Rhenium Adulteration The regulatory questions have gained significance following the investigation by Dainik Bhaskar , which examined whether rhenium, a heavy metal, could be mixed with gold to increase the weight of jewellery while escaping detection by commonly used purity-testing equipment.   The investigation, conducted in Jodhpur, involved mixing 1gm of rhenium powder with 7.830gm of 24-carat gold. The mixture was then used to make a traditional Rajasthani ornament after additional alloying metal was added.   The finished ornament weighed 9.580gm. According to the calculations reported by the newspaper, 7.830gm of this weight represented the original gold, putting the actual gold content at about 81.7%, or roughly 20-carat purity.   However, the ornament reportedly passed several tests. A hallmarking centre in Jodhpur issued a 916 mark, indicating 22-carat gold. A showroom testing machine reportedly showed 93.70% gold, 5.39% silver and 0.90% copper, without identifying rhenium. Another branded jewellery showroom also reportedly assessed the article as 22-carat gold.    It is important to distinguish this investigative experiment from evidence of widespread adulteration. The reported test does not establish that all hallmarked jewellery is adulterated or that rhenium is routinely being used across India. It does, however, raise questions about whether particular testing methods can identify a heavy metal deliberately introduced into a gold alloy.   How the Alleged Rhenium Method Works Rhenium is a dense metal, with a density slightly higher than that of pure gold. According to the Dainik Bhaskar investigation, this property could make it useful in an alleged adulteration method in which additional weight is introduced without an obvious change in the jewellery's physical characteristics.   The investigation reportedly traced a suspected supply route to an agent in Shenzhen, China, who allegedly claimed that his company manufactured rhenium powder for use in gold and had dealers in several Indian cities. A sample was subsequently procured through a Mumbai-based intermediary. These claims about the source and distribution network have not been independently established by government authorities.   The broader technical concern relates to the limitations of surface-based testing. X-ray fluorescence (XRF) equipment is widely used to check jewellery composition, but readings can depend on the equipment, its calibration, testing conditions and the material being examined.   BIS guidelines for recognised AHCs provide for XRF testing of jewellery and the collection of samples for further examination. The guidelines also distinguish XRF-based reporting from more comprehensive testing. This matters because a machine reading may not be equivalent to a complete examination of the entire article.   Hallmarking Alone Cannot Close the Enforcement Gap India's compulsory hallmarking regime was introduced to strengthen consumer confidence in gold purchases. It now covers 392 notified districts, while the country has more than 230,000 registered jewellery establishments.   The six-character HUID system has added another layer of traceability. Consumers can enter the HUID in the BIS Care application to verify details associated with a hallmarked article.   However, traceability and physical enforcement serve different purposes. An HUID can establish the identity and registration details of a hallmarked article, but it cannot independently establish that every part of the jewellery contains the declared quantity of gold if an adulteration technique has defeated the testing process used during certification.   This is where the CAG findings become important. If more than 81% of licensed jewellers were not subjected to surveillance in FY24-25, the regulator's ability to independently verify compliance across the market is constrained. The reported shortfall in AHC inspections also raises concerns about the testing and certification infrastructure.   The two developments therefore expose different weaknesses in the same system. A hallmark is only as reliable as the testing, certification and enforcement framework supporting it.   What Consumers Should Do The findings do not mean consumers should assume that hallmarked gold is unsafe. Hallmarking remains an important consumer protection mechanism, and the Dainik Bhaskar investigation represents a specific reported experiment rather than proof of widespread rhenium adulteration.   Buyers should purchase jewellery from established sellers, check the BIS hallmark and HUID, verify the HUID through the BIS Care application and insist that the invoice clearly records the weight and purity of the article.   Consumers who have serious doubts about a piece of jewellery should consider getting it examined at a BIS-recognised AHC rather than relying solely on an in-store purity-testing machine.   The larger issue emerging from the draft CAG audit and the newspaper investigation is one of regulatory confidence. India has built an extensive hallmarking framework to assure consumers that the purity stamped on jewellery can be trusted. The challenge is to ensure that this assurance is backed by regular inspections, reliable testing and effective action when irregularities are detected.   Until surveillance and testing become more robust, the gap between what a hallmark promises and what regulators can independently verify will remain a concern for millions of Indians who invest their savings in gold.
